snippets.snippet_text: The Bible gives us two verses about Noah's righteousness. The JST restores 120 years of prophetic ministry. Moses 8 reveals Noah preached with power, calling humanity to repentance with the same urgency as Enoch before him. The Holy Ghost strove with that generation until it finally "ceased striving"—language Mormon uses about our day in Mormon 8:28. Noah wasn't just a carpenter; he was a rejected prophet.
snippets.label: Restoration

snippets.snippet_text: "My spirit shall not always strive with man" uses the Hebrew word *dun*, meaning to judge, contend, or govern. The image is of God's Spirit actively wrestling for the souls of humanity, not passively waiting. There comes a point—after Enoch, after Noah's preaching, after 120 years—when the divine wrestling stops. That withdrawal of the Spirit, not the flood waters, is the real judgment.
snippets.label: Hebrew

snippets.snippet_text: "The Lord shut him in" is one of scripture's most tender phrases. Noah didn't seal the ark himself—God did. This same Hebrew verb (*sagar*) appears in Isaiah 45:1 when God opens doors for Cyrus, and in Matthew 25 when the door shuts on the foolish virgins. Jesus later says "I am the door" (John 10:9). God alone controls the threshold between safety and judgment, and He personally sealed Noah inside.
snippets.label: Cross-Ref

snippets.snippet_text: "Gopher wood" appears nowhere else in scripture, and no one knows for certain what tree it refers to. Ancient Jewish tradition suggests cypress; others argue for resinous cedar. But the word *kopher* (the root of "gopher") means "atonement" or "covering"—the same root as *kaphar*, used for the mercy seat in the tabernacle. The ark's wood may be unknown, but its symbolic function as protective covering is crystal clear.
snippets.label: Historical

snippets.snippet_text: Ham's sin after the flood was serious enough to merit a prophetic curse on Canaan, his son. The Hebrew suggests more than accidental viewing—the phrase "saw the nakedness of his father" may indicate a violation or mockery. This troubling text was tragically misused to justify slavery, yet Moses 7:8,12 clarifies that Canaan's curse was about priesthood restriction in ancient times, not skin color or perpetual servitude. Context matters desperately.
snippets.label: Prophetic

snippets.snippet_text: The first thing Noah did after 371 days in the ark was build an altar. Not inventory his supplies, not plant crops, not assess the damage. He worshiped. After trauma, after loss, after watching the world drown, his first act was covenant gratitude. For modern members emerging from their own trials—illness, divorce, loss—this sets the pattern: we rebuild altars before we rebuild houses.
snippets.label: Application
